name: Daria Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started playing for pay three years ago after working in a school kitchen. I play second clarinet in a community band, teach two new adults and record plain practice tunes. I finished secondary school, and the bandleader still checks difficult runs with me. Reeds are the thin strips that vibrate in a clarinet mouthpiece.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like alongside those calls?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58. My partner Luc works at a station ticket desk, our children are grown, and we rent a flat near the band hall. We have three months of expenses saved, my music pay is ordinary and a few centres hire nearby. I use AI now and then for timetable drafts after another player has tested a tool, then check the room and time myself.

say: I'd welcome **quicker notices** if the band gets the right room.
I'd tell players **live breathing** still matters in a clarinet line.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and Luc's wage cover a single late concert payment.
I use **AI occasionally** for draft timetables but check the signed hall sheet.
do: Confirm **four paid band calls** and two adult lessons tomorrow.
Save **forty** from a cleared concert fee after rent, heat and reed costs.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about moved dates, with enough savings for one delay.
S0.quote: A wrong notice can leave the band outside in the rain.
fieldNote: Her **junior clarinet work** pays typically and has a three-month buffer against one delay.
Her **occasional AI use** follows another player's trial and a signed-hall check.

steps.text: Confirm four paid band calls and two adult lessons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that quicker notices help if players get the right room. The clarinet still needs me to take a breath at the right moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI remains a small convenience, the band and beginner lessons should continue. Three months saved and Luc's desk wage cover one late concert payment, though rent still arrives on the same day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll confirm the next four paid band calls and my two adult lessons for the term. When the next concert fee clears, I'll put forty into our reserve after rent, heating and reed costs are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a moved concert but not trapped by one. A small tool change would leave me working at the music stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a concert moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall moved a spring concert and paid the next month. We used Luc's wage for food and did not touch the rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check a draft timetable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes use a draft timetable after a trusted player tries it. I compare the room and hour with the signed hall sheet. A wrong notice can leave the band outside in the rain.

say: I'd ask which **paid track hours** the hall plans to remove.
I'd bring **call sheets** to the musicians association before accepting lower fees.
think: About **one-quarter of my pay** from tracks and booking may shrink.
A **three-month reserve** covers a short gap but not repeated losses.
do: Compare **eight invoices** with the new schedule and bring them to the association this month.
Test a new **AI checker** after paid demonstration on my nameless part with paid-use licence and approved local storage.
Play **each suggestion manually**; require written learner consent and stop for wrong notes or files leaving the hall.
feel: I feel **anxious** because practice fees can fall while live rehearsals continue.
S1.quote: I would rather be paid for checking a part than be told the computer saved me time.
fieldNote: Her **practice recordings** make up a quarter of own pay, supporting anxiety despite three months saved.
Her **new checker trial** needs paid instruction, own nameless material, approved storage, manual playing and permission.

steps.text: Bring eight track invoices and new hall schedule to musicians association
Test checker after paid demo on own nameless part with paid-use licence and approved local storage
Play suggestions against score; stop for errors or storage breach
Require written learner consent before any pupil recording enters checker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the hall which paid practice-track and booking hours its software will remove. I would bring the band call sheets to the musicians association before agreeing to lower preparation fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a quarter of my pay comes from simple practice recordings and booking, and those could go first. Three months saved helps with a short gap, but not a term of missing fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare eight track invoices with the hall's new schedule and bring them to the association. In the first year of change, I'll attend a paid demonstration of a new AI note checker, then test my own nameless clarinet part only if its licence permits paid use and the hall approves local storage; I'll play each suggestion against the score and stop if notes change wrongly or a file leaves the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about likely lost track income even though the band still plays. I would rather be paid for checking a part than be told the computer saved me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a learner's recording enter that checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not upload a learner's recording without written permission. If the hall cannot keep files on its own system, I will use the paper part instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association can ask for a minimum paid preparation fee and a named person to approve file reuse. I'll bring the invoices rather than guess what the senior players earn.

I'd tell players **robot clarinets** follow thinking AGI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could remove tracks before robots play around 2031.
Our **three-month reserve** cannot replace lessons and tracks for long.

Keep **band/learners** until signed offer; if calls fall, request written rent terms before arrears and check charges before signing.
feel: I feel **anxious** about own fee loss, with some nearby centres and savings giving control.
S2.quote: A closed music-assistant vacancy is a memory, not a pay packet.
fieldNote: Her **2028 track loss** precedes robot clarinet playing around 2031.
Her **job move** needs both loss triggers, posted role, secondary-school acceptance, suitable hours and written net pay after travel.

steps.text: List band, lesson and track income; request signed next-season calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that AGI by 2028 could make practice tracks before robots can play clarinet around 2031. I would ask for live calls in writing while the hall still books us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The track fees could vanish at once, and some learners might buy a cheap digital practice guide instead of a lesson. Three months saved gives us a search period, but at 60 I still need paid hours rather than a promise about retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list band, lesson and track income and ask for signed next-season calls. In the first year after 2028, if track fees halve and lessons also fall, I'll apply for a posted music assistant role at a nearby centre only if it accepts secondary school and my experience, the hours suit me and written net pay after travel replaces the loss. I'll keep the band and present learners until another offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the loss, but a few centres and three months saved give me a route to ask. A closed music-assistant vacancy is a memory, not a pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there an open assistant job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A centre filled an assistant job last autumn. I would ask about the next posting rather than tell Luc I have a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if live calls also fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the band also cuts live calls, Luc and I will ask the landlord about temporary written terms before rent is late. We will check any added charges before signing.

I'd **price the class** before inviting anyone.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens tracks before robot players arrive around 2034.

Continue **after 2031** with six fees covering room/both musicians/preparation, paid lead, safe instruments and written terms; keep current band/lessons.

S3.quote: I can test a clarinet circle, but I will not use the rent account to pay its room.
fieldNote: Her **junior skill** limits her own teaching to first steps, with a paid lead supervising harder material.
She requires **inspected clarinets**, personal reeds and written learner consent before recording publicity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the arts centre five years is enough to test a paid beginner clarinet circle, if someone signs the room terms. I would price the class before inviting anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could make simple tracks and lesson plans, with robot players around 2034. Ordinary tools might cut recordings sooner, so a live class helps only if the fees cover my time while I learn to teach better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll run a six-week first-steps clarinet circle only if the centre signs room hire and insurance, six adults prepay enough for room, my teaching and preparation, and a paid lead player to supervise harder material, and six loan clarinets pass inspection. In the first year after 2031 I'll continue only while six paid places cover room and both musicians, written room terms hold, a lead remains available and instruments are safe; I will keep existing band calls and lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about putting a class together while track fees fade. I can test a clarinet circle, but I will not use the rent account to pay its room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are six loan clarinets safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre owns five safe loan clarinets and one awaiting repair. A technician must clear the sixth before I invite adults; if fewer than six pay or an instrument fails, I'll defer and refund prepayments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could recordings help advertise the circle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each learner will use a personal reed rather than share one. I will not post anyone's playing online without written permission.

I'd ask what **paid work** at 68 really looks like.
think: At **68 in 2036**, I cannot assume a pension pays rent.
**Track fees** may fade earlier, while robot players follow around 2039.
do: Request **pension statements** and a two-year written paid-call plan this year.
Build a **five-month reserve** from twenty percent of cleared extra concerts after rent, heat and instrument costs by 2036.
Apply **after 2036** if tracks fall and pensions leave a gap; require posted qualifying work, written replacement net pay and signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** because unchecked retirement income cannot guarantee rent.
S4.quote: I will not call an unchecked pension a wage.
fieldNote: Her **five-month goal** starts from three months and uses only extra concerts that actually pay.

steps.text: Request pension statements and a two-year written paid-call plan

Apply after 2036 if tracks fall and pension gap remains; require posted job accepting schooling/experience

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players ten years lets us ask what a paid music job at 68 really looks like. I would ask the hall for written part-time calls rather than assume a pension will fill the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036, with robot players perhaps arriving around 2039. I have not checked what retirement income Luc and I will have; track fees could go much sooner, so I need the facts before reducing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request our pension statements and ask the hall for a two-year written paid-call plan. By 2036 I'll aim to build five months of expenses from twenty percent of each extra cleared concert fee after rent, heat and instrument costs. In the first year after AGI, if track fees fall and the statements leave a gap, I'll apply for a posted part-time community music role only if it accepts secondary school and my experience, its hours suit me and written net pay after travel covers the loss; I'll keep current band and learners until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because a decade does not tell me whether retirement income covers rent. I can plan, but I will not call an unchecked pension a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five months already in the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have three months saved now, not five. I will count extra concerts only after they happen and pay, and leave the rent account alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a part-time music role available now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A nearby centre sometimes hires part-time helpers, but there is no role offered to me. I would check the actual posting and hourly pay before changing my teaching days.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because tracks and lessons could fall together before I find another paid centre job. Signed live calls, a real qualifying opening and pension statements would help Luc and me plan rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays for the sixth clarinet if the centre's loan fails. A class cannot sell a place that has no safe instrument.

headlineQuote: A class cannot sell a place that has no safe instrument.
portrait: Daria is a **58-year-old junior clarinetist** who began paid music after school-kitchen work and finished secondary school.
She and her partner have **grown children**, rent, three months saved and some nearby music options.
She uses **AI occasionally** after others test it, and checks a new note tool manually with storage and consent limits.
She pursues **paid beginner work** and checks retirement statements before reducing current calls.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could cut tracks and lessons together before another centre job opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed live calls**, a posted qualifying job and real pension statements would help plan rent.
